subject: chem
title: Stoichiometry
subtitle: Moles, empirical/molecular formulae, titrations and gas volumes.
concept: The mole links macroscopic mass to the number of particles. One mole contains 6.02×10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant).
Balanced equations give molar ratios — the key tool for all stoichiometric calculations.
Concentration, gas volumes (using molar volume 24 dm³ at RTP) and titration data all convert to moles for calculation.

notes.heading: Core Equations
items: n = m / Mr  (moles = mass / molar mass)
n = c × V  (moles = concentration × volume in dm³; divide cm³ by 1000)
At RTP (25°C, 1 atm): molar volume = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹, so n = V / 24
PV = nRT for non-RTP gas calculations (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

notes.heading: Empirical and Molecular Formula
items: Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
To find: convert % composition to moles by dividing by Ar, then divide by smallest.
Molecular formula = (empirical formula) × n, where n = Mr(molecular) / Mr(empirical).
Combustion data: burn compound, collect CO₂ and H₂O, calculate C and H moles, then O by difference.

notes.heading: Titration Calculations
items: Standard solution: accurately known concentration, made from a primary standard (e.g. anhydrous Na₂CO₃).
Steps: moles of known solution → moles of unknown (using ratio from equation) → concentration or mass of unknown.
Back titration: add excess reagent A to sample, titrate excess A against B to find how much A reacted with sample.

notes.heading: Percentage Yield and Atom Economy
items: Atom economy = (Mr of desired product / sum of Mr of all products) × 100
High atom economy = greener process (less waste).

definitions.body: The amount of substance containing 6.02×10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant).
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g mol⁻¹; numerically equal to the relative molecular mass.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
The percentage of the total mass of reactants that becomes the desired product: (Mr desired product / ΣMr all products) × 100.
A solution of accurately known concentration, prepared from a primary standard.

workedExamples.q: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass. Its Mr = 60. Find the molecular formula.

steps.text: C:1, H:2, O:1 → empirical formula CH₂O, Mr = 30

workedExamples.q: 25.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄ requires 30.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH to reach the endpoint. Find [H₂SO₄].

mistakes: Using cm³ instead of dm³ in concentration calculations — always divide cm³ by 1000.
Forgetting to use the molar ratio from the balanced equation before finding concentration.
Confusing empirical formula (simplest ratio) with molecular formula (actual number of atoms).
tips: Write out the full equation and mark the molar ratio before substituting numbers.
In combustion analysis, find C from CO₂ (1 mol CO₂ → 1 mol C), H from H₂O (1 mol H₂O → 2 mol H), then O by difference.
Atom economy favours reactions where only one product forms — addition reactions have 100% atom economy.

flashcards.a: Oxygen mass = sample mass − mass of C − mass of H (by difference).
